content: A page can be divided into sections by using specific section heading syntax. When creating sections, avoid using a single equals sign on each side of the text (e.g., `=text here=`), as this will create a title the size of the page name, which is automatically handled. Section numbering can be enabled through the Auto-number headings preference, which adds numbers to each section heading. It is recommended to use unique section names within a page, including for subsections, to avoid issues such as confusion after editing or ambiguous automatic edit summaries. Sections of a page can also include separate pages or templates without altering the page's appearance. This allows for independent edit histories and the ability to monitor sections separately. For example, if a template tag is placed in the third section, the first section of the template will be numbered as the fourth section. Any text in the template before its first section will appear as part of the section containing the template tag, and any text after the tag but before a new heading will appear as part of the last section of the template. While this can be done intentionally, it is generally better to avoid it. For pages with more than three headings, a Table of Contents (TOC) is automatically generated from the section headings unless user preferences disable it or the magic word `__NOTOC__` is added to the edit box. The TOC can be forced to appear even on pages with fewer than four headings by using `__FORCETOC__` or `__TOC__`. The placement of the TOC depends on the code used: `__FORCETOC__` places it before the first section heading, while `__TOC__` places it where the code is inserted. TOCs can also be placed in specific locations, such as on the right side or within a table cell, but this is only useful for long sections where the TOC occupies minimal space. Introductory text, known as the lead, may appear before the TOC. The depth of subsections displayed in the TOC can be globally limited using the `$wgMaxTocLevel` setting in the configuration file. For example, setting it to 3 will display only firstand second-level headings in the TOC. However, there is a known bug in some versions of the parser that causes limited TOC displays to render incorrectly. A solution for this issue is documented in bug report 6204. Each section in the HTML code has an anchor with name and id attributes corresponding to the section title. These anchors enable direct linking to specific sections. MediaWiki automatically uses these anchors when generating a TOC, allowing users to jump to a section by clicking its heading in the TOC. Manual linking to sections within the same page or another page is also possible using these anchors. Duplicate section names are appended with an underscore and a number (e.g., Example, Example_2, Example_3). However, editing sections with duplicate names can lead to confusion, as the edit summary may incorrectly reference the first instance of the name. Blank spaces as section headings result in non-functional TOC links. To create an anchor target without a section heading, a span tag can be used, but this may not work with very old browsers. Using date formatting in section headings complicates section linking. When linking to a section of a redirect page, the link corresponds to the section of the target page. However, renaming a section does not create a redirect, unlike renaming a page. Additionally, there is no separate backlink feature for sections; pages linking to a section are included in the list of pages linking to the entire page. Workarounds include linking to a page that redirects to the section, adding an anchor, or creating a separate page or template for the section. Redirect pages can be categorized by adding a category tag after the redirect command. If the redirect target is a section, the category page links to the section, but the section does not link back to the category unless explicitly done. Sections can be edited separately by clicking special edit links near the heading or by right-clicking the section heading, depending on user preferences. This is known as the section editing feature. Section editing is convenient for making changes without involving other sections and is particularly useful for large pages. The magic word `__NOEDITSECTION__` removes edit links but does not disable section editing entirely; right-clicking the heading or using the URL still works. Inserting a section can be done by editing the section before or after it or by merging it with the previous section by deleting the heading. Adding a section at the end can be done using a URL like `Sandbox&action=edit§ion=new`. On talk pages, a special link labeled + or Post a new comment is provided for this purpose, and the content typed in the Subject/headline box becomes the section heading and edit summary. Editing the introductory text before the first section heading can be done by specifying 0 as the section number in the URL (e.g., `Section&action=edit§ion=0`). A simpler way to obtain this link is to use any section edit link on the page and change the section number to zero. JavaScript can also create this URL. Templates like `{{Edit-first-section}}` and `{{Edit-top-section}}` create edit links for section 0 and can be copied to your wiki. Subsections are included in the part of the section being edited, but their heading format follows the absolute level. For pages with very large sections or no divisions, editing may be difficult due to browser or connection limitations. In such cases, one can append a section by specifying a large section number or append content to the last section without starting with a heading. If the wikitext of a large section is viewable, the page can be divided into smaller sections step by step, temporarily duplicating content. An explanation in the edit summary is helpful during this process. If a section heading is created conditionally using a parser function, the edit links for that and subsequent sections may edit the wrong section. This occurs because section counting for edit links is done after expanding parser functions, while the edit page counts only static sections. To avoid this, either refrain from creating sections via parser functions or disable section editing. To edit a footnote rendered in a section, edit the section containing the footnote mark referring to it. For more information, see Help:Footnotes. Separate pages have advantages such as independent edit histories, faster loading, and the ability to categorize them individually. However, one large page with sections offers faster and more convenient navigation, especially for searching within the page. An alternative is to compose a page using the template feature, which allows easy searching within the combined rendered page but not the combined wikitext. A disadvantage of this method is the need to provide a title for each page. To create a heading that does not appear in the TOC, use specific HTML or extensions. However, HTML headings now appear in the TOC by design. Extensions can provide the ability to create non-TOC headings. For example, a simple extension can add tags for H1, H2, H3, and H4 headings that do not show up in the TOC.
